source.title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize: A Loss Landscape Perspective On Data
source.authors: R. Fan; Bryce Sandlund; Ling-Chin Ko

record.tranche_reason: Measures filter-normalized basin volumes and their relation to test performance across dataset sizes, training methods and batch sizes; this is a different measure from the claim versions’ specific sharpness metrics.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own volume, test-accuracy and training-loss results. Results it cites from prior work, including random-label memorization, are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares CNN and MLP test accuracy (V3) and SGD and AdamW test accuracy (V4). Its batch-size experiment bears on V5, but the supplied text does not establish a fixed epoch budget. Its basin-volume experiments do not test V7's specific within-convolutional-family relationship between magnitude-aware sharpness and generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors find that training usually selects relatively large-volume minima, while models trained on larger datasets can generalize better yet occupy smaller basins in a smaller-data landscape. They distinguish this from SAM and small-batch results, where larger basins accompany better accuracy, and from grokking, where volumes decrease as accuracy improves. They qualify the volume explanation with noisy exceptions in swiss roll and modulo arithmetic.
record.recipe_differences: Measures filter-normalized Monte Carlo basin volume across dataset sizes, optimizers, batch sizes and architectures; it does not reproduce the original memorization/generalization, width, convolutional-bias, dropout or example-removal interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The relation between volume and test accuracy depends on dataset and training-data size; the swiss roll relative-volume result can change with loss threshold. Volume scaling is sensitive to loss threshold, perturbation count, filter normalization, architecture and training method. The paper reports differing trends for dataset-size comparisons, optimizer variations and batch sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM increases basin volume and modestly improves MNIST MLP accuracy; the text reports its largest accuracy improvements on low-data swiss roll.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding SAM to AdamW can increase basin volume and improve test accuracy in the studied MLP settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Across training-data sizes, better-generalizing image models can occupy smaller basins in the same small-data loss landscape.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Filter-normalized basin volume need not positively track test accuracy when comparing models trained on different amounts of image data.

fits_no_version.finding: Volume–accuracy relationships vary with dataset and training-data size, and swiss roll basin ordering can depend on the loss threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Basin-volume relationships with test accuracy depend on the problem, data regime, and measurement threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: During modulo-arithmetic grokking, basin volumes shrink while test accuracy improves and training loss changes little.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Improved generalization during grokking can accompany decreasing basin volume.

record.problems: The authors note limitations of star-convex basin volume estimation, including high-dimensional Monte Carlo sensitivity to rare flat directions and scale invariance concerns. They report substantial seed variability in swiss roll and modulo arithmetic; some figure comparisons have no numerical values in the text. SVHN at 60,000 examples had only two models that reached sufficiently low training loss within the allotted epochs.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Figure 26 batch-size results are reported qualitatively in the text, with no exact batch sizes or values. Figures 13, 27–31 and other appendix plots include additional results, but many are not numerically described in the text; the extraction preserves the relevant text-described outcomes and the stated tabular values.

untested.parts: No paired natural-label and fixed-random-label fitting and held-out accuracy experiment; random-label capacity is cited.
No width sweep beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Local connectivity is not isolated; sparse fully connected networks and initialization from trained CNNs are not tested. CIFAR-100 and SVHN architecture comparisons are not reported.

Limited versus broader tuning, matched training performance, language benchmarks, switching optimizers, and decoupled weight decay as an intervention are not tested. AdamW uses PyTorch defaults; the SGD tuning protocol is unspecified.

The fixed epoch budget required to interpret the batch-size comparison is not established. Workload thresholds, language models, longer training, warmup, learning-rate scaling, and normalization or regularization adaptations are not tested.

No reported test of magnitude-aware sharpness ranking generalization gaps among one convolutional family at similarly low training loss, or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures. Filter-normalized basin volumes and MLP accuracy comparisons address a broader flatness hypothesis.
No removal and retraining experiment based on example memorization.

record.verdict_notes: No V5 verdict is warranted without the epoch-budget condition. The paper's counterexamples concern a broad flat-minima hypothesis and should not be presented as challenges to V7's narrower empirical claim. All assessments use only the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization are cited as prior work, not tested here.
No width sweep across the zero-training-error threshold.
The paper compares MLP and CNN results on MNIST and CIFAR10, but does not isolate local connectivity or test sparse fully connected networks or CNN initialization.
Reports an MNIST AdamW/SGD comparison, but does not test the cited image and language benchmarks, limited versus broader tuning, switching optimizers, or decoupled weight decay as an intervention.
Reports batch-size effects on MNIST, but does not evaluate language models, a workload-dependent threshold, or adaptive large-batch recipes.

Uses filter-normalized basin volume and other perturbation-radius summaries, not Jiang et al.’s exact magnitude-aware sharpness measure or comparison against norm- and margin-based measures. It does not hold training loss similarly low across the full set of comparisons.

rows.subject: MNIST, MLP (SGD)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD; compared with the MNIST MLP trained with AdamW.
rows.locator: Table 1; Appendix C.2; Appendix F, Table 2
rows.note: The authors state SGD tends to generalize better and find sharper minima; the accuracy differences shown are small.
rows.check: SGD exceeds AdamW by only 0.2 and 0.6 percentage points; uncertainty is not supplied. Remove V7: this MLP accuracy comparison does not measure the claimed convolutional-family sharpness–gap relationship. Optimizer tuning and matched training performance are not documented.

rows.subject: MNIST, MLP (SAM)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with AdamW + SAM and compared with vanilla AdamW.
rows.value: SAM achieves improved test accuracy and finds larger minima than vanilla AdamW; numeric values not stated
rows.note: The paper describes the improvements as modest for test accuracy; no numerical values are provided in the text.
rows.check: Adding SAM to AdamW does not compare adaptive optimization with SGD. The MLP basin-volume result also does not test V7. Contrary to the row, Tables 1–2 supply MNIST SAM accuracies: 97.8% / 67.8%, versus AdamW's 97.7% / 67.5%. Keep this as a separate SAM finding.

rows.subject: MNIST models trained with varying batch sizes
rows.operation_detail: Varied batch size on a fixed number of examples and measured minima volume and test accuracy.

conditions.value: different batch sizes; exact values not stated
10 different model and data split seeds

rows.value: Large batch gradient descent tends to find smaller minima; test accuracy is inversely correlated with batch size.
rows.note: The authors describe the relationship; exact batch-size values and accuracy figures are not given in the text.
rows.check: The authors explicitly report decreasing test accuracy with increasing batch size, but neither Appendix D nor the supplied methods specifies whether epoch budgets are held fixed. Fixed example count does not establish fixed epochs. Remove V7: these are not the specified convolutional-family sharpness–gap measurements.

rows.subject: MNIST MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared minima trained on different dataset sizes in the loss landscape formed by 60 examples.
rows.measure: Basin volume / perturbation distance and test accuracy
rows.value: The 60,000-example minima are smaller in the 60-example landscape, while the 60-example minima have poorer generalization.
rows.note: The paper says perturbations to low-data minima travel further than perturbations to full-data minima, while the latter generalize better.
rows.check: The reversed volume–accuracy relationship is reported correctly, but concerns an MLP across training-data sizes, using basin volume in a small-data loss landscape. It does not measure V7's specified within-family sharpness–generalization-gap relationship.

rows.subject: CIFAR10 MLP and CNN
rows.size_stated: MLP: 2 hidden layers of 512, 256 neurons; CNN dimensions not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared minima from different training-data sizes in smaller-data loss landscapes.
rows.measure: Basin volume / perturbation distance and test accuracy
rows.value: The figure description says the difference between minima trained on the largest and smallest datasets is evident.
rows.note: The figure caption does not give a direction or numerical result for the CIFAR10 comparison.
rows.check: Section 5.2 supplies the direction omitted by the row: CIFAR10 minima trained on less data tolerate larger perturbations while generalizing worse. The row also combines MLP and CNN subjects without establishing that Figure 16 includes both. These cross-data-size basin comparisons do not establish V7's specified sharpness–gap relationship.

rows.subject: Swiss roll MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared perturbation distances for minima trained on the largest and smallest datasets in a 20-example loss landscape.

conditions.value: choice can change which minima appears larger

rows.value: Only intermediate minima are significantly smaller; choice of loss threshold can change which minimum appears larger.
rows.note: The authors explicitly qualify the relative-size conclusion by the loss threshold.
rows.check: Swiss roll MLP perturbation-radius ordering and its threshold sensitivity do not test V7's convolutional-family claim.

rows.subject: Minima trained on fixed datasets with AdamW and SAM
rows.operation_detail: Compared minima volume with test accuracy across model seeds on fixed datasets.

conditions.value: MNIST: 1,000 and 11,000 examples; swiss roll: 50 and 800 examples

rows.value: The impact of volume on test accuracy is noisy and depends on problem and training dataset size.
rows.note: The paper reports a noisy, condition-dependent relationship; it also says models with higher test accuracy generally occupy slightly larger volumes as additional MNIST data is added to the 1,000-example models.
rows.check: This combines several fixed-data seed experiments and reports basin volume versus accuracy, without the specified convolutional family, matched low training losses, or generalization-gap measurements. Its noisy relationship cannot establish or limit V7.

rows.subject: Modulo arithmetic (base 97) model
rows.operation_detail: Extended training from 500 to 5,000 epochs and tracked volume and test accuracy.
rows.measure: Training loss, basin volume and test accuracy
rows.value: Training loss changes almost not at all, volumes shrink significantly and test accuracy increases dramatically.
rows.note: This is a time-course result; exact values are not stated.
rows.check: The reported grokking trajectory is correct, including nearly unchanged training loss. However, a modulo-arithmetic MLP becoming sharper during training is outside V7's specified convolutional-family comparison.
